guides.title: Cyprus With Kids: A Practical Family Travel Guide
guides.summary: Cyprus with kids: shallow Blue Flag beaches, three waterparks, zoos, boat trips and Troodos day plans, plus the car seat law and health tips families need.
guides.html:
Cyprus works well for a family holiday because the things children need most sit close together. Beaches shelve gently into warm, clear water, longer journeys across the south can take around 2.5 hours, and English is widely spoken. This guide covers the calm beaches, waterparks, zoos and boat trips, ruins that hold a child's attention, Troodos with young ones in tow, rainy-day backups, and the practical details on car seats, sun and health.

Where to base yourself

The best family base depends on your children's age and how much you plan to drive. Protaras and Ayia Napa have the gentlest beaches and two of the three waterparks within reach. Paphos pairs sandy bays with walkable ruins and its own waterpark. Larnaca sits next to the main airport, suiting short stays.

  • Youngest children, beach-focused: Protaras, for shallow water and a short walk to everything.
  • Mixed ages, beach plus sightseeing: Paphos, where the seafront and ancient sites sit close together.
  • Short trip or late flight: Larnaca, a few minutes from the airport with a long promenade.
  • Cooler escape in summer: the Troodos mountains, several degrees cooler than the coast.

Distances matter more with children in the car than for adults alone. Count on roughly 2.5 hours from Paphos Airport to Protaras (Paphos to Limassol is about 90 km, Limassol to Protaras roughly 1h 50 – 2h 15), and a bit over 2 hours from Troodos to the east coast. Most families do better splitting a week between two bases, for example a beach stretch followed by a few nights in Paphos, with day trips filling the gaps.

The calmest beaches for children

Two beaches stand out for families and both hold Blue Flag status, signalling clean water, lifeguards and safety equipment in season. Fig Tree Bay at Protaras has soft sand, a gradual entry and water shallow enough for small children to wade a long way out, with a small islet just offshore that confident swimmers reach by a short swim on a calm day. On the west coast, Coral Bay sits in a sheltered horseshoe with the same easy entry and sunbeds backed by cafes.

A few more bays suit families. Makronissos Beach near Ayia Napa is a string of small protected coves with calm water, and Finikoudes Beach in Larnaca runs alongside a palm-lined promenade for a beach day and an ice cream stroll. Lifeguard seasons vary by beach; the official tourism listing gives June to October for the beach in Larnaca.

Whatever beach you pick, treat the sun seriously. In June and July the UV index around midday is routinely extreme and unprotected skin can burn quickly, so plan the strongest sun (roughly 10am to 3pm) around shade or lunch. Bring a parasol or beach tent (except at Lara, where umbrellas and tents are banned from June to September), reapply sunscreen often, and pack a hat for every child. Water shoes save small feet on hot sand and the occasional rocky patch.

Waterparks worth the day

Cyprus has three sizeable waterparks, one on each side of the island, so a family based almost anywhere is within reach of one. WaterWorld in Ayia Napa is the best known, billed as Europe's largest themed waterpark and built around an ancient Greek mythology theme with rides from gentle children's pools up to steep drops for teenagers. It runs daily, roughly 10am to 5pm in the shoulder months and 10am to 6pm from June to August, tickets around EUR 50 adult and EUR 30 child aged 3 to 12, often with a second-visit offer worth checking.

Limassol's option is Fasouri Watermania, west of the city near Kolossi, open May to October with 30 different slides and attractions, one of Europe's larger wave pools, a lazy river about 400 metres long said to be the biggest in Cyprus, and a children's pool that stays knee-deep throughout. Entry runs around EUR 30 over 12 and EUR 17 for a child. Supervision rules are strict: under-12s need an accompanying adult, under-8s must be supervised at all times, and children aged five and under need an adult within three metres of them in the water.

Paphos has Aphrodite Waterpark, the biggest in the region, open from spring into early November with hours shifting by month. Prices start from around EUR 20 for a child and EUR 36 for an adult, and a family ticket for two adults and three children runs from around EUR 115. Arrive close to opening for shaded loungers, and check the operator's site for the day's hours since all three parks vary.

Zoos and animal days

For a change of pace from sand and slides, Cyprus has three solid animal attractions across the south. Pafos Zoo is open daily year-round from 9am, closing anywhere from 5pm in winter to 7pm in August, and charges around EUR 19 to 20 adult and EUR 12 to 13 child, with parrot and owl shows at its amphitheatre. Near Larnaca, Camel Park in Mazotos is the only camel park on the island, home to more than 100 animals including camels, ostriches and ponies. Limassol Zoo, rebuilt inside Limassol Municipal Park, is the budget option: adult entry around EUR 5, children around EUR 2, with keeper-led feeding sessions.

Boat trips and turtle watching

Boat trips are a hit with children who tire of sitting still on a beach. From Protaras Pier or Paralimni Marina, a glass-bottom boat sails several times a day so children watch marine life without getting wet, from around EUR 20 adult and EUR 10 child, up to EUR 25 and EUR 15 for a longer sailing. From Ayia Napa harbour, the pirate-themed Black Pearl cruise is a fuller morning out, roughly four hours with swim stops and lunch included, for around EUR 45 adult and EUR 25 child. Both leave from points walkable for a family based in Ayia Napa or Protaras.

Between roughly May and September, loggerhead and green turtles nest at Lara Beach on the Akamas peninsula near Paphos, with hatchlings mostly emerging in August and September. There is no organised night-watch tour, so treat turtle watching at Lara as a possible bonus rather than a booked activity: with good timing you may spot roped-off nests or, rarely, hatchlings crossing the sand. Lara has no shops, shade or toilets, and the last stretch needs a sturdy vehicle. From 1 June to 30 September umbrellas, tents and sunbeds are banned there and the beach is closed from an hour before sunset, so plan a short daytime visit. The flamingos at Larnaca Salt Lake draw winter visitors, roughly November to March.

Ruins that work with short attention spans

Cyprus has serious archaeology, and a few sites hold children's interest because there is space to roam and something visual to look at. Keep visits short, go early before the heat, and pick sites with a clear story or a striking feature.

  • Ancient Kourion near Limassol has a Greco-Roman theatre carved into a cliff above the sea, an easy shape for children to grasp, with mosaics nearby.
  • Kolossi Castle is a compact medieval tower you can climb to the roof, small enough to explore in half an hour.
  • Paphos Archaeological Park has flat paths between covered mosaic houses, so the going underfoot is easier than at most ruins.
  • Tombs of the Kings lets children walk down into underground courtyards cut from rock, which feels like an adventure, though the ground is uneven.

Aphrodite's Rock on the Paphos to Limassol road makes a quick photo and paddle stop tied to a memorable myth, and Omodos village in the Troodos foothills has a cobbled square, a monastery and space to run around.

Troodos with kids

The mountains are worth a day even with young children, mostly for the drop in temperature and space to run around rather than hiking distance. Near the summit of Mount Olympus there is an easy, largely flat circular walk for young legs, well short of the longer routes serious hikers take. Troodos village square has a proper playground under the pines, ringed by cafes and restrooms. Near Pano Platres, the walk to Millomeris Waterfall is short and manageable, about 20 minutes each way from a car park with a toilet and cafe; the tougher Caledonia Falls trail beyond it suits older children. Snow is possible in winter, a genuine novelty worth checking conditions for.

Rainy or too-hot day options

Cyprus is dry most of the year, but a cool indoor stop still helps on a scorching August afternoon or a wet spell in winter. The Fairytale Museum in Nicosia's old town, near Paphos Gate, is a genuine child-oriented museum with storytelling and workshops; entry runs around EUR 5, under-4s free, hours vary by season. Nicosia, Limassol and Larnaca also have indoor soft-play and trampoline venues for an overheated afternoon.

Driving and getting around

A hire car is the practical way to travel as a family, letting you reach beaches and sites on your own timetable and carry beach gear. Cyprus drives on the LEFT, the same as the UK, familiar to British visitors and worth a moment's thought for everyone else. Roads are generally good, though Troodos hill roads are narrower and slower than coastal motorways.

Child car seats are a legal requirement. Under the Road Safety Law (174/1986, Article 15), a child shorter than 150 cm must travel in an approved restraint suited to the child's size and weight and fitted to the manufacturer's instructions. From 135 cm the law allows the adult belt in a rear seat of a car with belts fitted throughout, though a well-fitting approved booster is still the safer choice. A rear-facing seat must never be used in front of an active airbag, and Road Safety Cyprus publishes the current approval standards and the rules on young children in the front seat. Driving a child without the correct restraint carries a fixed penalty of EUR 150 plus three to six penalty points, doubled for a repeat offence within three years. Most hire companies rent seats, but book ahead since stock is limited in peak season, and bringing a seat you trust from home is often the surest option.

Health, heat and practical tips

Cyprus is an EU member and the standard of care is good. The single emergency number is 112, and operators speak English. EU and UK visitors should carry a valid EHIC or GHIC for state healthcare, alongside travel insurance, which covers private clinics and repatriation that the card does not. There is no permanent 24-hour pharmacy, but a rotating duty system guarantees one open every night in every region, until roughly 10pm in winter and 11pm in summer, posted on every closed pharmacy's door.

Tap water across the south meets EU drinking-water standards and is officially safe to drink, though the taste leads some residents to prefer filtered or bottled water; for infant formula, use freshly boiled water from the cold tap, still at least 70C when preparing the feed; bottled water is not recommended because it is not sterile and may contain too much sodium or sulphate. Summer afternoons are hot enough to wilt small children, so build the day around a cool middle, treating 10am to 3pm as the window to avoid. The currency is the EURO, and plugs are type G, the UK three-pin, at 230 to 240 volts.

NeedFamily tip
SunBeach in the morning and late afternoon; rest or eat indoors between 10am and 3pm.
WaterTap water is safe across the south; carry refillable bottles to avoid dehydration.
FoodA souvla grill plate or grilled halloumi suits most children; meze lets fussy eaters pick.
StrollerOld-town lanes and ruins are uneven; a carrier beats wheels at archaeological sites.
MoneyCards are accepted widely; keep some EUR cash for small beach kiosks and village cafes.

Local food is easy with children. Halloumi appears at almost every meal, loukoumades are warm honey doughnuts that win over most kids, and kleftiko lamb suits younger eaters. Most tavernas are relaxed about children, and some places, such as Pelican Restaurant, have a dedicated kids menu.

Sample family day plans

A beach-and-waterpark base might run: a slow morning on the sand before the sun peaks, then an afternoon at the waterpark once the worst heat has passed. A Paphos-based day could pair an early morning at the archaeological park with an afternoon swim, leaving the zoo for another day. For a cooler change of scene, drive up to Troodos for a walk and playground time before heading back down. Spacing one bigger outing every other day keeps energy levels steady.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which part of Cyprus is best for families with young children?

The east coast around Protaras and Ayia Napa is generally easiest, thanks to shallow, gently shelving beaches and easy access to WaterWorld. Paphos suits families who want to mix beach time with ruins, while Larnaca works well for short stays close to the airport.

Which waterpark should we choose?

Choose the one closest to your base. WaterWorld in Ayia Napa is the best known and bills itself as Europe's largest themed waterpark, Fasouri Watermania near Limassol is the largest park in Cyprus by area and has the biggest lazy river, and Aphrodite Waterpark is the most convenient if you are staying in Paphos. All three have dedicated toddler pools.

Is a car seat required by law in Cyprus?

Yes. A child shorter than 150 cm must use an approved restraint suited to their size and weight; from 135 cm the law allows the adult belt in a rear seat of a car with belts fitted throughout, though an approved booster remains the safer option. Road Safety Cyprus sets out the rules on young children in the front seat and the approval standards that count. The fixed penalty for not using the correct seat is EUR 150 plus three to six penalty points, and it doubles for a repeat offence within three years.

Can we get by without a rental car?

It is possible if you stay entirely on the east coast, since Protaras Pier, Ayia Napa harbour and several beaches are walkable, and boat trips leave on foot. Reaching Troodos, Lara Beach or the far side of the island without a car is much harder.

Is the tap water safe for children to drink?

Yes, municipal tap water across the south of Cyprus meets EU drinking-water standards and is officially safe. Many residents still prefer filtered or bottled water for taste, but bottled water is not recommended for making up infant formula because it is not sterile and may contain too much sodium or sulphate; use freshly boiled water from the cold tap, still at least 70C when preparing the feed.

What should we do about the midday sun with young children?

Treat roughly 10am to 3pm as the window to avoid direct sun, especially in June and July when the UV index is routinely extreme. Plan beach time for the morning or after mid-afternoon, use a beach tent where allowed (not at the Lara turtle reserve in summer), and reapply sunscreen often.

Are there good rainy or too-hot indoor options?

Yes. The Fairytale Museum in Nicosia's old town is a genuine child-oriented museum with storytelling, themed exhibitions and workshops, and entry runs around EUR 5. Nicosia, Limassol and Larnaca also have indoor soft-play and trampoline venues that work well for an overheated afternoon or an unexpected wet spell in winter.

Can we realistically see turtles at Lara Beach?

You might, but it is not a guaranteed or bookable experience. Loggerhead and green turtles nest at Lara roughly from May to September, with hatchlings mostly emerging in August and September, and there is no organised night-watch tour, so any sighting comes down to timing and luck rather than a booked activity.
guides.bestTime: Late May to June and September, for warm sea and lighter heat

guides.title: Things to Do in Cyprus: A Complete Guide
guides.summary: Things to do in Cyprus span UNESCO-listed Roman mosaic villas uncovered in 1962, the top-ten Zenobia wreck dive, Troodos trails and east-coast beaches.
guides.html:
Cyprus packs a lot into a small island. You can stand inside a Roman villa floored with 1,800-year-old mosaics in the morning, swim off a quiet cove at midday, and drink local wine in a mountain village by evening. The Republic of Cyprus (the government-controlled south) covers everything below, and most of the highlights sit within a 90-minute drive of each other. The country uses the euro, drives on the left, and runs on the EU emergency number 112. Greek and Turkish are the official languages, but English is spoken almost everywhere. Here is how to spend your time well.

See the ancient sites and mosaics

Cyprus has been settled, fought over, and rebuilt for thousands of years, and the archaeology is genuinely first-rate rather than a token stop. Start in the west.

The Paphos Archaeological Park at Kato Paphos has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1980. Its four Roman villas, including the House of Dionysos, preserve some of the finest mosaic floors in the eastern Mediterranean, depicting mythological and hunting scenes. The first mosaics here were uncovered in 1962 by a farmer ploughing his field. A short walk away, the Tombs of the Kings is a necropolis of underground chambers cut straight into the rock, used by Paphos officials rather than actual royalty.

East of Paphos, near Limassol, Ancient Kourion sits on a cliff above the sea, with a Greco-Roman theatre still used for performances and more mosaic floors in the House of Eustolios. Nearby Kolossi Castle, a 13th-century Crusader stronghold, is tied to the production of Commandaria, the sweet dessert wine. In the south, Choirokoitia is a Neolithic settlement, also UNESCO-listed, where reconstructed round houses show how people lived here more than 9,000 years ago.

For Aphrodite mythology, Aphrodite's Rock (Petra tou Romiou) on the Paphos-Limassol road is the sea stack where the goddess is said to have risen from the foam. You can swim at the pebble beach below, listed separately as Petra tou Romiou beach.

Spend time on the beaches

The east coast around Ayia Napa and Protaras has the clearest, palest water and the most reliable sand. Nissi Beach is the famous one, with a sandbar you can wade across to a small islet. Fig Tree Bay at Protaras is calmer and good for families, and Konnos Bay sits in a sheltered horseshoe between the two towns. For something quieter, Sunrise Beach and Makronissos Beach spread the crowds out.

Further west, Coral Bay near Paphos is the main resort beach, while Lara Beach on the Akamas peninsula is an undeveloped stretch where loggerhead and green turtles nest. Finikoudes Beach runs along the Larnaca seafront in the middle of town, and Governor's Beach between Limassol and Larnaca has dark sand framed by white chalk cliffs.

Head into the Troodos mountains

The Troodos mountains are the green, cool centre of the island and a complete change of pace from the coast. Mount Olympus (Chionistra) is the highest point in Cyprus at 1,952 metres and holds enough snow in winter to support a small ski area on its Sun Valley and North Face slopes. The rest of the year it is a hiking base.

Several waymarked nature trails circle the upper slopes with long views, but they do not all begin in the same place: the 14 km Atalanti loop starts at Troodos Square, while the 7 km Artemis loop starts about 300 metres from where the Chionistra road meets the Troodos to Prodromos road. Serious walkers should look at Troodos mountain hiking for the full network. Across the wider Troodos region you will also find painted Byzantine churches, ten of which are UNESCO-listed for their frescoes.

The mountains hold two of the island's most important monasteries. Kykkos Monastery, the wealthiest on Cyprus, is famous for its gold mosaics and an icon attributed to Saint Luke. Cap a mountain day at Omodos village, a stone wine village with a cobbled square, or push north to the remote Cedar Valley, home to thousands of native Cypriot cedars and the occasional mouflon (the island's wild sheep).

Drink the wine

Cyprus has one of the oldest wine cultures in the world, and the indigenous grapes (Xynisteri for whites, Mavro and Maratheftiko for reds) make it worth more than a single tasting. The villages on the southern slopes above Limassol are the heart of it.

  • A Limassol wine villages tour links several small producers across the Krasochoria (literally "wine villages") in one trip.
  • An Omodos village wine tour focuses on the most visitor-ready of those villages, with cellars off the main square.
  • Commandaria wine tasting covers the sweet amber wine that has been made in the same region for centuries and is one of the world's oldest named wines still in production.

If your visit lands in late September, the Limassol Wine Festival in the Municipal Gardens is a long-running celebration with tastings and food, usually running for around ten days into early October. Read more on the regional Commandaria entry before you go.

Dive the Zenobia wreck

Off Larnaca lies one of the best wreck dives anywhere. The MS Zenobia, a Swedish-built roll-on roll-off ferry, capsized and sank in Larnaca Bay in June 1980 on her maiden voyage. She rests on her port side at around 42 metres, with the upper starboard side reachable from about 16 to 18 metres, and her cargo of articulated lorries is still chained on the decks. The Times and many dive publications rank her among the top ten wreck dives in the world.

Because the ship is so large, there is something here for every level, from guided dives for newly certified divers over the shallower hull to technical penetration dives through the car decks. Book through a Larnaca operator for scuba diving the Zenobia wreck; certification and a buddy check are standard. If you are not a diver, the rest of the coast still has plenty of accessible snorkelling.

Watch the wildlife and walk the coast

In winter the Larnaca Salt Lake fills with rain and draws thousands of greater flamingos, typically from November to March, with the biggest numbers between December and February. View them from the marked paths rather than approaching, and aim for early morning or late afternoon light. A salt lake flamingo birdwatching outing pairs the lake with the Hala Sultan Tekke mosque on its shore.

On the Paphos side, the Akamas peninsula is the wildest corner of the country. Lara Beach hosts a turtle conservation project, and you can join turtle watching at Lara in the nesting season. The Avakas Gorge nearby narrows to a slot, but its walking trail is currently temporarily closed, and the Blue Lagoon at the tip is reached on foot, by 4x4, or on a Blue Lagoon boat cruise from Polis and Latchi. On the east coast, Cape Greco has sea caves, cliff paths, and a natural rock arch.

Take day trips between the towns

Distances are short, so basing yourself in one town and exploring the rest is easy. Here is a rough sense of driving times.

FromToApprox. drive
LarnacaNicosia45 minutes
LarnacaAyia Napa / Protaras45 minutes
LimassolTroodos (Mount Olympus)1 hour
LimassolPaphos1 hour
PaphosPolis / Latchi40 minutes

The capital, Nicosia, deserves a day for its Venetian walls and museums. A Nicosia old town walking tour of the old town covers the restored Ledra Street area and the Cyprus Museum's archaeology collection. From the east coast, a Cape Greco boat cruise reaches sea caves the road cannot, and families gravitate to WaterWorld waterpark in Ayia Napa. From Paphos, an Akamas jeep safari reaches the gorge, the Baths of Aphrodite, and remote bays in one trip.

Eat as you go

Cypriot food rewards grazing. A meze meal brings a long parade of small plates, and the staples are worth seeking out: grilled halloumi, slow-roasted kleftiko lamb, souvla (large cuts cooked slowly over charcoal), and loukoumades honey dumplings to finish. Order what the village around you is known for and you will rarely go wrong.

Quick planning notes

  • When to go: April to June and September to October are the most comfortable. July and August are hot but reliable for the sea; winter suits the mountains, the wine villages, and the flamingos.
  • Getting around: A hire car is the practical choice for the interior and the Akamas. Remember to drive on the left.
  • Money: Cyprus uses the euro. Cards are widely accepted, but carry some cash for village tavernas and small producers.
  • Essentials: Plug type G (the UK three-pin), 230 to 240 volts. Dialling code is +357. Emergency number is 112.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need to see the best of Cyprus?

Five to seven days covers the highlights well: two or three nights on the coast (Paphos or Ayia Napa/Protaras), a night or two in the Troodos mountains, and a day for Nicosia's old town. Ten days to two weeks lets you add the Akamas peninsula, a wine-village crawl, and the Zenobia dive without rushing.

Do you need a car to see the ancient sites and the Troodos mountains?

For the Troodos villages, the wine region, and remote spots like the Avakas Gorge and Cedar Valley, yes, a hire car is the practical choice since bus service thins out fast once you leave the coast. The main archaeological parks (Paphos, Kourion, Choirokoitia) and coastal towns are reachable by bus or organised tour if you would rather not drive, and Cyprus drives on the left.

Is Cyprus worth visiting if you don't want a beach holiday?

Yes. Between the UNESCO mosaics and Neolithic site, the painted Byzantine churches and monasteries of the Troodos, the wine villages above Limassol, and the Zenobia wreck dive, there is a full week of inland and cultural content that does not depend on the coast at all.

Do you need to be a certified diver to see the Zenobia wreck?

Yes. Introductory try-dive programmes (PADI Discover Scuba Diving, SSI Basic Diver) are capped at 12 metres, which is shallower than the highest point of the wreck, so the Zenobia itself is a dive for certified divers. Larnaca operators set their own entry bar, often Advanced Open Water or equivalent, and the deeper hull and car-deck penetration dives at around 42 metres need the relevant wreck and technical training on top of that.

What's the best month to combine Troodos hiking with beach time?

April, May, June, September and October give warm enough sea temperatures for swimming while keeping the mountain trails comfortable rather than baking. In peak July and August the coast is hot but reliable, while the Troodos altitude offers a cooler break from it; midwinter suits the mountains, the wine villages, and the Larnaca Salt Lake flamingos rather than the beach.

Pick two or three of these threads (ancient sites, beaches, mountains, wine, diving) rather than trying to do everything, and a week on the island feels generous rather than rushed.
guides.bestTime: April to June and September to October

guides.title: Troodos Trip Planner: Wine Villages, Churches & Kykkos
guides.summary: Plan a Troodos trip village by village: the Commandaria wine route, ten UNESCO painted churches, Kykkos Monastery, where to stay and how long to spend.
guides.html:
The mountain heart of Cyprus

The Troodos mountains form the forested interior of the Republic of Cyprus, rising between Limassol on the south coast and Nicosia to the north. The range tops out at 1,952 metres on Mount Olympus, and the slopes are covered in black pine, cedar and golden oak. The air is noticeably cooler than the coast, which is why Cypriots have escaped here each summer for generations. Stone villages cling to the hillsides, Byzantine churches hide in the valleys, and small wineries press grapes grown above 600 metres.

The high ground around Mount Olympus is protected as the Troodos National Forest Park, roughly 90 square kilometres of protected pine forest with marked trails protecting river headwaters. You can reach the central villages in about an hour from Limassol or 50 minutes from Nicosia. Cyprus drives on the LEFT, and a hire car is the only realistic way to explore.

The hill villages

The villages are the reason most people climb into the Troodos. Each has a square, a coffee shop and a church, and many keep working trades such as wine or lace.

Omodos

Omodos sits at about 800 metres on the southern slopes, roughly 42 km northwest of Limassol. The cobbled main square fronts the Monastery of the Holy Cross (Timios Stavros), which holds a fragment of the True Cross and, by tradition, part of the Holy Rope said to have bound Christ, plus a relic venerated as the skull of the Apostle Philip. Legend says villagers repeatedly saw fire and smoke among the bushes and dug up a cave containing a cross, over which the first chapel was built. Small museums cover the national struggle, lacemaking and rural life, and the lanes hold wineries and lace shops. Read more in our Omodos village guide or join an Omodos wine tour.

Kakopetria

Kakopetria stands at about 667 metres in the Solea valley, its highest village, where the Kargotis and Garillis rivers meet to form the Klarios river. The old quarter has narrow stone paved lanes and restored houses with wooden balconies over the water. Its landmark is the Mylos tis Gonias, the Corner Mill, a watermill built in 1754 to grind wheat and barley, which stopped after the Second World War and has since been restored beside the first stone bridge. On Milos Street beside it, The Old Mill ties into that watermill history. Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis, one of the painted churches, sits about 5 km outside the village; see the Kakopetria page for more.

Platres

Platres (Pano Platres) sits higher, around 1,200 metres on the southern flank of Mount Olympus, about 9 km from Troodos and roughly 39 km from Limassol by road. It has been a hill resort since Britain took control of Cyprus in 1878, growing colonial era hotels in the early 1900s. New Helvetia, founded in 1929, is the oldest hotel in continuous operation in Cyprus. Forest Park Hotel, built in the 1930s, is where local history says Daphne du Maurier wrote part of "Rebecca" during a 1936 to 1937 stay. Platres straddles a perennial mountain stream, and its walk to the Caledonia and Millomeris waterfalls makes a good hiking base.

Pedoulas and the Marathasa valley

Pedoulas sits at about 1,100 metres in the Marathasa valley, roughly 75 km from Nicosia with a comparable drive from Limassol. It is Cyprus's main cherry growing area and hosts an annual cherry festival, usually in June, drawing thousands of visitors. Its Archangel Michael church, dated 1474, is one of the painted churches. Nearby Kalopanayiotis is known for stone houses, sulphur springs and a Venetian bridge over the Setrachos river.

The painted churches

The Troodos region holds ten small Byzantine churches and monasteries on the UNESCO World Heritage List as the Painted Churches in the Troodos Region: nine added in 1985, plus the church at Palaichori in 2001. From plain stone or timber exteriors, often with steep pitched roofs to shed snow, the interiors open into walls covered in frescoes painted between the 11th and 17th centuries. Highlights include:

  • Asinou (Panagia Phorviotissa) near Nikitari, with some of the finest 12th century frescoes on the island
  • Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis (St Nicholas of the Roof) near Kakopetria, named for its second protective roof
  • Panagia tou Araka near Lagoudera, richly painted in 1192
  • Archangel Michael at Pedoulas, dated to 1474
  • The Monastery of Agios Ioannis Lampadistis at Kalopanayiotis, three churches under one large timber roof, believed founded in the 11th century

Several churches are kept locked, with a key holder usually living nearby and no fixed admission, though a small donation is expected, and photography is often restricted. Plan a route rather than expecting to see all ten in a day; pairing the Marathasa villages with Kalopanayiotis is one practical way to see several at once.

Kykkos Monastery

The Holy Monastery of Kykkos is the wealthiest and best known monastery in Cyprus. It stands at about 1,318 metres on the northwest side of the range, about 13 km from Pedoulas, letting you combine it with the Marathasa villages in one loop. Tradition ties its founding to Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, said to have sent an icon of the Virgin Mary to Cyprus after a hermit healed a member of his family; the monastery holds that icon, attributed to the Apostle Luke, and today's buildings are later work, since fire destroyed the original several times. Archbishop Makarios III, the republic's first president, began his career here as a novice.

Entry is free; the museum charges a small fee, commonly around EUR 5, subject to change. Typical hours, as of 2026, run 10:00 to 16:00 from November to May and 10:00 to 18:00 from June to October, open year round except public holidays. Modest dress is required, shorts are not permitted, and shoulders and knees must be covered; free cover up robes are available at the entrance. See the Kykkos Monastery page for details.

Mount Olympus and hiking

Mount Olympus, locally called Chionistra (Greek for snow), is the highest point in Cyprus at 1,952 metres. A British radar station occupies the summit itself, so you cannot stand on the very top, but the loop trail around it gives wide views over the forest and both coasts on clear days. See the Mount Olympus page for orientation. The forest park has 10 nature trails, covering about 57.6 km. Signed routes near the summit and around Platres, part of Troodos mountain hiking, include:

  • Artemis trail, easy, circling Olympus at roughly 1,850 metres, about 7 km, typically 2.5 to 3 hours
  • Atalante trail, easy to moderate, a contour route from Troodos Square, around 14 km clockwise through pine and cedar forest, about 4 hours
  • Caledonia trail, difficult, between Pano Platres and the Caledonia waterfall along the Kryos river, about 3 km one way, roughly 2 hours, with a steady uphill grade
  • Millomeris trail, short but rated difficult, about 1.2 km one way from Pano Platres, with steep, rocky stretches, to a waterfall often called the tallest in Cyprus at about 15 metres, under an hour

Trails are best from April to June and September to November. Carry water, since taps are scarce, and wear proper shoes since paths are rocky. In a cold winter the upper slopes hold enough snow for a short ski season, run on four lifts across two zones, typically January to March (more below).

The wine villages and Commandaria

The southern slopes of the Troodos are the Krasochoria, the densest cluster of wineries on the island, growing indigenous Xynisteri (white) and Mavro (red) grapes up to around 1,000 metres. Omodos, Koilani, Vouni and Lofou belong to this wine belt, outside the narrower legal zone for the region's most famous product.

That product is Commandaria, an amber dessert wine made by leaving grapes to overripen on the vine, then sun drying them after harvest to concentrate the sugar before fermentation. A 1990 Cyprus law defined a protected zone of 14 villages entitled to the name, including Agios Georgios, Kalo Chorio, Doros, Laneia, Louvaras and Silikou, and it carries designation of origin status in the EU, the US and Canada. In December 2025, Commandaria was added to UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, Cyprus's seventh element on that list, and tradition traces it back millennia, including a legend it was served at Richard the Lionheart's wedding in Limassol in 1191.

You can tour the area on a Limassol wine villages tour, taste the sweet wine on a Commandaria tasting, or build your own loop through Omodos, Koilani, Vouni and Lofou; our weekend wine villages guide covers a longer route. Many small producers welcome visitors without booking, though calling ahead is wise outside summer.

Seasons in the Troodos

Summer is the main draw for anyone escaping the coastal heat: while Limassol and Larnaca sit in the low 30s Celsius (high 80s to low 90s Fahrenheit) through July and August, the higher villages run noticeably cooler. Spring and autumn bring the best hiking weather and clearest views, plus the cherry festival window in Pedoulas. Winter is genuinely cold at altitude and brings real snow most years, feeding the ski operation above; roads into high villages sometimes get restricted to vehicles carrying chains or four wheel drive during snowfall, so check road condition reports before a winter trip.

Practical driving and where to stay

Troodos roads are narrow and winding with sharp hairpins: drive slowly, use a low gear on descents, and sound the horn on blind corners, a habit locals still practice. Fuel stations are sparse once you leave the main towns, so fill the tank first. As of 2026, pump prices run roughly EUR 1.55 to 1.75 per litre for unleaded 95 and EUR 1.948 for diesel on average including taxes as of 21/09/2026; cards are widely accepted but rural stations can be cash only. Most rental cars carry red plates, which makes them easy to spot as hire cars. Between November and March, snow and ice are a real possibility on higher roads.

A single day covers one valley comfortably: a village and a winery, one painted church, a short walk. Staying overnight lets you add a second valley and catch villages before day trippers arrive. The Cyprus Agrotourism Company, set up in 1996, represents more than 150 members, many traditional stone village houses renovated for guest stays. Kalopanayiotis, Kakopetria and Lofou have clusters of these, booking up during the cherry festival and summer weekends, so reserve ahead.

What to eat

Mountain cooking leans on slow roasting and the village oven. In Pano Platres, Psilo Dendro has run as a working trout farm and restaurant for more than 50 years, grilling trout from its own tanks for outdoor diners under the trees; it is primarily a warm season, lunchtime stop, so check ahead in winter. Village tavernas serve meze, small hot and cold dishes built around local lamb and pork with fresh bread and dips. Look for these specifically:

  • Kleftiko, lamb sealed in a clay oven until it falls off the bone
  • Souvla, large chunks of meat turned slowly over charcoal
  • Halloumi, the grilling cheese, often served with village bread

Practical planning

DetailInformation
CurrencyEuro (EUR), card widely accepted, carry cash for key holders and small wineries
Getting thereHire car from Limassol (1 hour) or Nicosia (50 minutes); driving is on the LEFT
Best monthsApril to June and September to November for hiking; January to March for a chance of snow
Emergency112 across Cyprus
PowerType G plug, 230 to 240V
LanguageGreek, with English widely spoken

The Troodos pair well with the coast. Combine the mountains with Limassol for an easy two centre trip, or add the western valleys near Polis and Latchi. With only a day, focus on one valley: Omodos and a winery, one painted church, and a short walk near Platres.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a car to visit the Troodos mountains?

Yes, effectively. Public buses reach some larger villages, but service is thin and not built around combining several stops in one trip. A hire car lets you pair a village, a church and a trail in a day, the only practical way to reach most trailheads.

How long does it take to drive from the coast to the Troodos?

From Limassol, the central villages are about an hour's drive; from Nicosia, around 50 minutes. Platres is roughly 39 km from Limassol, Kakopetria roughly 50 km, and Pedoulas roughly 75 km from Nicosia, so allow extra time for winding roads.

Can you still ski in the Troodos mountains?

Yes, when there is enough snow. The Cyprus Ski Club runs four lifts above Troodos Square across two zones, typically within a January to March window, but the season depends on snowfall each year and slopes can stay closed if conditions are insufficient.

Do you need to visit all ten painted churches?

No. The ten UNESCO painted churches are spread across the range rather than clustered, so seeing all in one trip is unrealistic. Pick two or three on your route, such as Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis near Kakopetria and the Archangel Michael church at Pedoulas, and save the rest for later.

What should I wear to visit Kykkos Monastery?

Modest dress is required for everyone: shorts are not permitted, and shoulders and knees must be covered. If you arrive under dressed, free cover up robes are available at the entrance, so it is not a reason to skip the visit.

Is Commandaria the same as the wine made in the krasochoria villages?

Not exactly. The krasochoria is the broader band of wine producing villages, including stops like Omodos and Koilani. Commandaria is a specific product legally tied to a narrower list of 14 villages defined by Cyprus law, so the two overlap but are not identical.

What is the best base for exploring the Troodos, Platres or Omodos?

Platres suits hikers and anyone chasing cooler summer air, since it sits higher and puts the Caledonia and Millomeris waterfalls within a short walk. Omodos suits a shorter visit focused on wine tasting, easy to reach and leave in half a day. Many visitors combine both.

Are the mountain roads safe to drive for a first time visitor to Cyprus?

They are manageable if you drive cautiously. The roads are narrow and winding with sharp hairpins, so keep your speed down, use a lower gear on descents, and sound the horn on blind corners as locals do. In winter, snow and ice are realistic, so check conditions between November and March.

guides.title: Where to Stay in Cyprus: Best Base by Traveller Type
guides.summary: Choosing where to stay in Cyprus: compare Paphos, Limassol, Larnaca, Ayia Napa, Protaras, Nicosia, Polis and the Troodos by area, vibe and airport.
guides.html:
Cyprus is small, but it is not small enough to treat as one place. The Republic of Cyprus (the government-controlled south) runs from the white-sand party beaches of the southeast to the painted churches of the Troodos mountains, and the drive between them takes a couple of hours. Where you sleep shapes the whole trip: the beach outside your door, how far you drive to the sights, and how loud the night is. This guide compares the main bases by traveller type, then drills into the sub-areas of Paphos, Limassol and Larnaca, so you choose on fit, not airfare.

The two airports, and why they matter

Cyprus has two international airports, and your base partly decides which you use. Larnaca (LCA) is the closest gateway to Ayia Napa, Protaras and Nicosia. Paphos (PFO) is the natural arrival point for Paphos and Polis. Pick the wrong side and you add a long transfer at both ends.

  • From Larnaca airport: Larnaca town about 15 minutes, Ayia Napa and Protaras roughly 45 minutes, Limassol around an hour, Nicosia about 45 minutes.
  • From Paphos airport: Paphos about 15 to 20 minutes, Limassol around an hour, Ayia Napa and Protaras roughly two and a half hours, so do not fly into Paphos for an east-coast holiday. Polis and Latchi are about 50 to 55 km away, an hour by car.

Cyprus drives on the left, the currency is the euro (EUR), the dialling code is +357, and the emergency number is 112. Greek is official and English is widely spoken. If hiring a car, see renting a car in Cyprus.

The bases, side by side

BaseBest forNearest airportCharacter
PaphosHistory, couples, relaxed familiesPaphos (PFO)Slower west coast, ruins and harbour
LimassolFood, culture, central touringLarnaca or Paphos (~1h each)City energy, marina, wine country inland
LarnacaShort transfers, easygoing budgetsLarnaca (LCA)Walkable seafront, no-fuss town
Ayia NapaNightlife, young groupsLarnaca (LCA)Party resort with top sand beaches
ProtarasFamilies, quiet beach daysLarnaca (LCA)Calm, family resort next to Ayia Napa
NicosiaCity break, culture, no beachLarnaca (~45 min)Divided capital, walled old town
Polis / LatchiQuiet, Akamas base, walkersPaphos (~1h)Small northwest coast towns, harbour
TroodosWalkers, cool air, villagesLarnaca or PaphosPine forest, monasteries, wine villages

Paphos: history and a slower pace

Paphos suits travellers who want ruins and beach in one place without rushing. Its ancient sites have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, and the headline sights sit close together: the Roman mosaics of Paphos Archaeological Park by the harbour and the rock-cut Tombs of the Kings nearby. The coast is rockier than the southeast, but the Akamas wilderness with Lara Beach and Avakas Gorge is on the doorstep.

Kato Paphos, Ktima and Coral Bay

"Paphos" splits into two parts plus a resort strip up the coast. Kato Paphos, the lower coastal town, is where almost everyone stays: harbour, beach, archaeological park and most restaurants within walking distance, though harbour-front dining is priced for tourists. Ktima, the upper old town, sits roughly 2 to 4 km inland and uphill, linked to the harbour by bus 610, more affordable but with no sea access. Coral Bay, about 11 to 12 km north in Peyia, within Akamas municipality, is a separate resort strip of golden sand and shallow water, reachable by bus 615. Paphos overall suits couples and families who like a poolside apartment over a club strip.

Limassol: the cosmopolitan, central choice

Limassol is the largest coastal city and the best base for food and central touring. It mixes an old town around a medieval castle with a modern marina, livelier than Paphos or the east. The Roman city of Kourion and Crusader Kolossi Castle sit just west, and the wine villages inland, including Omodos, are covered in weekend krasochoria wine villages.

Old town and marina versus the eastern hotel strip

Limassol splits into two stay zones. The old town and marina, around Limassol Marina, the castle and the promenade, has cafes, boutiques and city buzz, suited to nightlife and walking without a car. The eastern hotel strip (Amathus, Dasoudi and Germasogeia) stretches east of the centre, with Germasogeia and Dasoudi closer in and hotels farther east about 11 km from the town centre, a concentration of beachfront pools and spas. A local bus links the zones in about 20 minutes; a single ticket runs around EUR 2, worth checking fares. Limassol is the most central base for day-tripping the south, and its grey-gold sand and shingle beaches draw people who value city life over a postcard beach. It hosts the country's oldest wine festival and largest carnival.

Larnaca: short transfers and an easy budget

Larnaca is the practical pick for minimal hassle and a gentle budget. The airport is barely 15 minutes from the palm-lined Finikoudes promenade, and the town is walkable, with the Church of Saint Lazarus central and the salt lake on the edge, where flamingos gather in winter. Divers come for the Zenobia wreck.

Finikoudes, Mackenzie and Oroklini

Larnaca's coastline is not just Finikoudes. Finikoudes is the central promenade beach, walking distance of the old town. Mackenzie Beach lies a short way down the coast toward the airport end, lively with clubbing at night, and an easy walk or drive from the centre. Oroklini (also Voroklini), about 8 km northeast, roughly 15 minutes by car or bus, is quieter and residential, with its own family beach, a nearby wetland where flamingos winter, and family hotels. Larnaca suits budget travellers and anyone using the city as a launch pad to Ayia Napa, Nicosia or the Troodos; see Cyprus on a budget for costs.

Ayia Napa vs Protaras: same coast, opposite moods

These two sit a few kilometres apart on the southeast tip and share the island's best white-sand beaches, but pull different crowds.

  • Ayia Napa: the party base, famous nightlife, plus Nissi Beach, Makronissos, the WaterWorld waterpark and Cape Greco. For young groups, not quiet evenings.
  • Protaras: the calmer, family version, built around Fig Tree Bay and coves like Konnos Bay, a gentle resort strip rather than clubs.

Both are about 45 minutes from Larnaca airport, and you can visit one from the other in minutes, so many travellers pair them.

Ayia Napa's winter reality

Ayia Napa is strongly seasonal. Most nightclubs, beach bars, water-sports operators and restaurants close from roughly November until the season restarts near Easter, deep winter running December to March. The town keeps running year-round for residents (supermarkets, pharmacies, a reduced bus, a few tavernas), but some hotels shut entirely for January and February, so confirm dates before booking outside summer. A modest 2025-2026 push has hotels staying open extra weeks each end of season, though closures persist; April to June and September to October stay reliable.

Nicosia: the city-break case, no beach

Nicosia is the only major Cyprus base with no coastline, landlocked near the island's centre, with the nearest beaches roughly 45 to 50 km away, generally under an hour's drive. What it offers instead is the island's strongest city-break case. The old town, the walled city around the Venetian Walls (built by the Republic of Venice in 1567-1570, a circle roughly 5 km around with eleven bastions), suits a car-free 2 to 3 night stay: cafes, restaurants, museums and boutique stays cluster around Ledra Street, which runs toward the UN buffer zone, and the Laiki Geitonia quarter. This guide covers the Republic-controlled south only, treating Nicosia purely as a city-break base. A walking tour and the Fairytale Museum suit a short stay.

Polis and Latchi: the quiet northwest

Polis and Latchi are two closely linked small towns on the northwest coast, about 3 km apart, the natural base for the Akamas Peninsula and the Baths of Aphrodite. Latchi has a fishing harbour expanded into a small marina lined with fish tavernas, where boat cruises to the Akamas and Blue Lagoon depart; Polis is quieter, a "real Cyprus" town. This is the most remote popular base, about 50 to 55 km from Paphos airport. It suits walkers and bird-watchers wanting unspoilt quiet, pairing well with a few nights in Paphos or Limassol.

Troodos: cool air, walking and villages

The Troodos mountains are the base for a different Cyprus: pine forest, painted Byzantine churches, wine villages and summer temperatures cooler than the coast. Walkers come for trails around Mount Olympus and Troodos hiking routes, and Kykkos is the island's most important painted monastery.

Agrotourism: staying in a village

The distinctive way to sleep in the Troodos is agrotourism: restored stone village houses converted into guesthouses, often with fireplaces, courtyards and mountain views. Cyprus Agrotourism, a non-profit set up in 1996 following a Cyprus Tourism Organisation initiative, coordinates bookings for more than 150 rural members, mostly stone-house stays plus boutique hotels and wine producers. Villages known for it include Kakopetria, above the Kargotis river, Kalopanagiotis, known for sulphur springs and the UNESCO-listed Church of Agios Ioannis Lampadistis, and Lofou, known for narrow lanes of stone houses. It is good value against coastal pricing, typically a 1 to 2 night add-on with Omodos and Commandaria wine tasting from Limassol, Paphos or Larnaca.

Hotel styles worth knowing about

Adults-only hotels operate in Ayia Napa, Paphos and Protaras for a child-free stay. Boutique hotels in restored buildings are a current category in the old-town cores of Nicosia, Limassol and Larnaca. Self-catering apartments and villas are well established, especially in Larnaca and Paphos, valued for a kitchen and space.

How to choose

  • Families: Protaras for calm sand, Coral Bay for pool complexes.
  • Nightlife: Ayia Napa, outside winter shutdown.
  • Couples, first-timers: Kato Paphos for history, Limassol old town for buzz.
  • Budget: Larnaca or Ktima.
  • City break: Nicosia's old town for 2 to 3 nights.
  • Unspoilt coast: Polis and Latchi, near the Akamas.
  • Cool air: a couple of nights of agrotourism in the Troodos.

The most common split: one week of beach, two or three nights inland or in a second city. A hire car turns almost any base into a launch pad for the rest of the island; read the first-timers guide before committing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best area to stay in Cyprus for a first visit?

Kato Paphos or Limassol's old town are the easiest first bases. Kato Paphos keeps harbour, beach, archaeological park and restaurants within walking distance, so you need not drive on your first days on the left. Limassol old town offers similar walkability, more restaurant variety.

Should I stay in Larnaca or Ayia Napa?

Choose Larnaca for short transfers, a walkable centre and an easygoing budget, and Ayia Napa for the island's best-known nightlife and white-sand beaches. Larnaca suits solo travellers and budget couples; Ayia Napa suits young groups wanting a loud, lively night.

Is Kato Paphos or Ktima better to stay in?

Kato Paphos suits visitors who want to walk to the harbour, beach and Roman ruins and do not mind tourist-strip prices. Ktima, roughly 2 to 4 km uphill and inland, suits travellers wanting a local, affordable base, happy to take the 610 bus to the harbour or drive to the coast.

Is Ayia Napa open in winter?

Only partly. Most nightclubs, beach bars and water-sports operators close from around November until the season restarts near Easter, and some hotels shut entirely for January and February. The town stays open year-round for residents, so check a hotel's dates before booking outside summer.

Do I need a car if I stay in Nicosia?

Not for the old town itself. The walled city around the Venetian Walls, including Ledra Street and Laiki Geitonia, is compact and walkable, with museums, cafes and boutique stays close together. You will want a car or transfer to reach the coast, roughly 45 to 50 km away.

What is agrotourism in the Troodos, and is it worth it?

Agrotourism means staying in a restored stone village house, booked through the Cyprus Agrotourism network of more than 150 rural members. It is generally good value against coastal pricing and offers a quieter experience in villages like Kakopetria, Kalopanagiotis or Lofou, usually a 1 to 2 night add-on.

destinations.name: Ayia Napa
destinations.tagline: Southeast resort of white-sand bays, Cape Greco and nightlife
destinations.summary: Ayia Napa is Cyprus's busiest summer resort: white-sand beaches led by Nissi Beach, the sea caves and trails of Cape Greco, and the island's best-known nightlife.
destinations.html:
Ayia Napa sits at the far southeast of Cyprus, in the Republic-controlled south of the Famagusta District, and is the island's busiest summer resort. It grew from a fishing village around a 15th-century monastery into a beach town famous for fine white sand, shallow turquoise water and a concentrated nightlife scene. In peak season it runs lively and young, but the beaches and the surrounding coast appeal far beyond the club crowd.

The signature beach is Nissi Beach, a Blue Flag stretch of roughly 600 metres of pale sand with a sandbar to a small islet. Quieter sands lie nearby at Makronissos Beach and Landa Beach. East of town, Cape Greco is a national forest park of sea caves, low cliffs and walking trails, with the sheltered cove of Konnos Bay to the north, towards Protaras.

What to do

  • Swim at Nissi Beach, then try the calmer sands of Makronissos.
  • Walk the nature trails and explore the sea caves, or use the specialist cycling paths of Cape Greco national forest park.
  • Swim and snorkel in the clear, sheltered water of Konnos Bay.
  • Visit the old monastery on the central square before the evening crowds arrive.

The town centre packs in bars and clubs around the main square, which is the heart of the nightlife. Away from that, family resorts, water parks and a small harbour give Ayia Napa a broader appeal, and the shoulder months of May, June, September and October are calmer and cooler than high summer.

Neighbouring Protaras and its Fig Tree Bay are about 10 to 12 kilometres north and run a quieter, more family-focused scene. Larnaca and its airport are roughly 45 minutes west along the motorway, which makes transfers straightforward.

destinations.name: Larnaca
destinations.tagline: Southeast city with the main airport, palm promenade and salt lake
destinations.summary: Larnaca is the arrival point for most visitors: Cyprus's main airport, the palm-lined Finikoudes promenade, the Church of Saint Lazarus and a winter salt lake of flamingos.
destinations.html:
Larnaca sits on the southeast coast and is where most visitors first land, as it holds Cyprus's main international airport (LCA), just a few kilometres from the centre. The city is low-key and walkable, built around the palm-lined Finikoudes seafront promenade and a sandy town beach, with an old town of churches and a small fort behind it. It makes an easy, central first base for the island.

The historic anchor is the Church of Saint Lazarus, a stone Byzantine church in the old town built over the reputed tomb of Lazarus. South of the city, the Larnaca Salt Lake fills with winter rain and draws flocks of flamingos from roughly November to March; the Hala Sultan Tekke mosque stands on its shore. The town beach, Finikoudes Beach, runs the length of the promenade, with Mackenzie Beach closer to the airport.

What to do

  • Walk the Finikoudes promenade and visit the Church of Saint Lazarus in the old town.
  • Watch the flamingos at the Larnaca Salt Lake in winter, beside Hala Sultan Tekke.
  • Swim at Finikoudes Beach or the broader Mackenzie Beach near the airport.
  • Dive the Zenobia wreck offshore, one of the Mediterranean's best-known dive sites.

Larnaca's central location makes it a useful hub. The eastern resorts of Ayia Napa and Protaras are about 45 minutes east, while Limassol and the capital Nicosia are each roughly an hour away. That keeps day trips short in every direction.

The city has a relaxed, lived-in feel rather than a heavy resort scene, which suits travellers who want culture, easy beaches and good food without the crowds of the far southeast. The old Turkish quarter, the fort and the marina area reward an unhurried wander on foot.

photo.alt: Amazing townscape in Larnaca, Cyprus.

destinations.name: Limassol
destinations.tagline: South-coast city of castle, marina, wine villages and Kourion
destinations.summary: Limassol is Cyprus's largest coastal city: a medieval castle, modern marina and long seafront, with the Roman ruins of Kourion and Troodos wine villages a short drive away.
destinations.html:
Limassol (Lemesos) lies on the south coast and is the largest city on the Cyprus shoreline, the commercial and cruise hub of the island. It mixes an old town around a small medieval castle with a long modern seafront, a new marina of restaurants and yachts, and a business district of high-rise towers. The setting is practical rather than postcard-pretty in places, but it puts a lot of Cyprus within easy reach.

The medieval castle in the old town houses the Cyprus Medieval Museum and is tied by tradition to the marriage of Richard the Lionheart in 1191. West of the city, the Greco-Roman city of Kourion spreads along clifftops above the sea, with a restored theatre still used for performances. Nearby stands Kolossi Castle, a Knights Hospitaller stronghold rebuilt in the 15th century and linked to the island's sweet Commandaria wine.

Around Limassol

  • Walk the seafront and marina, then visit the castle and old town lanes.
  • Tour the ruins and theatre at Kourion, then see Kolossi Castle nearby.
  • Spend a relaxed beach day at Governor's Beach or Lady's Mile Beach.
  • Drive up to the wine village of Omodos for tavernas and family wineries.

Limassol's beaches are mostly grey-gold sand and shingle rather than the white sand of the east, so many visitors come here for the city, food and culture as much as the swimming. The wine country of the southern Troodos slopes climbs just inland, and the city hosts a large wine festival and carnival each year.

It sits roughly midway along the coast, about an hour from both Paphos and Larnaca airports by motorway, and is a convenient base for Aphrodite's Rock and the Troodos Mountains. That central position makes it a strong base for touring the whole south.

destinations.name: Nicosia
destinations.tagline: Inland capital of Venetian walls, Ledra Street and museums
destinations.summary: Nicosia (Lefkosia) is the inland capital: a walled old town with Venetian ramparts, the pedestrian Ledra Street and the Cyprus Museum's leading archaeology collection.
destinations.html:
Nicosia (Lefkosia) is the capital of Cyprus and the only major city on the island that sits inland, on the central Mesaoria plain. Its old town is enclosed by a star-shaped ring of Venetian walls built in the 16th century, and inside them a grid of narrow lanes holds churches, museums, craft workshops and cafes. This guide covers the south side, the part of the city within the Republic of Cyprus.

The main artery is the pedestrian Ledra Street, lined with shops and cafes, which runs through the heart of the old town. Just off it stand restored Ottoman and medieval buildings, including the Faneromeni church and the lanes of the Laiki Geitonia quarter. The Cyprus Museum stands just outside the walled centre, the island's leading archaeology collection, with finds spanning the Neolithic to the early Byzantine period.

What to do

  • Walk Ledra Street and the lanes of the old town inside the Venetian walls.
  • See the island's top archaeology at the Cyprus Museum.
  • Visit the cathedral of Saint John and the Byzantine museum in the Archbishopric quarter.
  • Browse shops near Faneromeni square.

Nicosia is a working capital rather than a beach town, so it suits a day or two of history, museums and food rather than a full holiday. It is also the only divided capital in Europe, with the buffer zone running through the centre; the south side covered here is fully part of the Republic and easy to explore on foot.

The city sits about an hour inland from Larnaca and Limassol, which makes it an easy day trip from either coast. The painted churches and villages of the Troodos Mountains begin to climb to the southwest, including the hilltop Kykkos Monastery.
destinations.bestMonths: April to June, September to October

destinations.name: Paphos
destinations.tagline: West-coast UNESCO city of Roman mosaics, harbour and rock tombs
destinations.summary: Paphos pairs a UNESCO archaeological park of Roman mosaics with a working harbour, Tombs of the Kings and Cyprus's quieter western coast. The natural base for history and west-coast beaches.
destinations.html:
Paphos sits on the southwest coast of Cyprus and works as the natural base for a history-led trip. The archaeological sites at Kato Paphos and Kouklia have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, recognised for its layered Greek, Roman and early Christian past. The old town sits uphill in Ktima (Pano Pafos), while the tourist area of Kato Pafos runs down to a small harbour ringed by tavernas and a medieval castle.

The headline site is the Paphos Archaeological Park in Kato Paphos, where the floors of grand Roman villas survive as detailed mosaics of mythological scenes. A short walk north, the Tombs of the Kings is a rock-cut necropolis carved into the coastal stone, its underground chambers styled like houses for the dead. Outside town, Aphrodite's Rock marks the legendary birthplace of the goddess on the road toward Limassol.

What to do

  • Walk the mosaics of the archaeological park, then continue to the Tombs of the Kings.
  • Swim and snorkel at Coral Bay, the main sandy beach north of town.
  • Drive into the Akamas for the turtle-nesting sands of Lara Beach and the Avakas Gorge walk (currently temporarily closed; check official updates before visiting).
  • Eat fresh fish around the harbour below the castle in the evening.

Paphos has its own airport (PFO) just east of town, which keeps transfers short. The coast here is rockier than the southeast, but you still get good swimming at Coral Bay and a string of small coves. The town suits couples, families and first-time visitors who want culture and beach time in one place, at a slower pace than the eastern resorts.

From here it is an easy run north to Polis and Latchi and the Akamas peninsula, or east along the motorway to Limassol and the Roman city of Kourion. Inland, the painted churches and wine villages of the Troodos Mountains are within a day trip.

destinations.name: Polis & Latchi
destinations.tagline: Northwest gateway to the Akamas, Blue Lagoon and Baths of Aphrodite
destinations.summary: Polis and the harbour of Latchi are the quiet northwest of Cyprus: the Akamas peninsula, the Blue Lagoon by boat, the Baths of Aphrodite and unhurried fishing-village dining.
destinations.html:
Polis and the neighbouring harbour of Latchi (Latsi) sit on the northwest coast of Cyprus, in the Paphos District, and offer the quietest, most low-rise corner of the island. Polis is a relaxed inland town with a pedestrian square of tavernas, while Latchi, about five minutes away, is a small fishing harbour known for seafood and boat trips. Both serve as the gateway to the wild Akamas peninsula, the largest undeveloped stretch of coast in the south.

The best-known target is the Blue Lagoon, a sheltered turquoise inlet on the Akamas coast reached by boat from Latchi or by 4x4 track. On the way sits the Baths of Aphrodite, a small natural grotto and spring tied to the goddess legend, with a nature trail leading along the headland. Further south down the rugged coast lie the turtle-nesting sands of Lara Beach and the Avakas Gorge.

What to do

  • Take a boat from Latchi to swim at the Blue Lagoon.
  • Walk the trail from the Baths of Aphrodite along the Akamas headland.
  • Eat fresh fish at the harbourside tavernas in Latchi in the evening.
  • Drive the rough Akamas tracks to Lara Beach and check access to the Avakas Gorge nature trail (temporarily closed).

This is the place to come for nature and quiet rather than nightlife or big resorts. The Akamas is a protected area of cliffs, gorges, sea caves and unspoilt beaches, popular for hiking, snorkelling and boat trips. Accommodation is mostly small hotels and villas, and the pace stays slow even in high summer.

Polis and Latchi sit about 45 minutes north of Paphos and its airport, which makes them an easy add-on to a west-coast trip. From here the rest of the Akamas, and quieter beaches than the busy southeast, are right on the doorstep.

photo.alt: Rocky coastline with turquoise waves crashing ashore.

destinations.name: Protaras
destinations.tagline: Family resort of Fig Tree Bay and calm southeast beaches
destinations.summary: Protaras is the calmer, family-focused neighbour of Ayia Napa: led by the white sand of Fig Tree Bay, a string of sheltered coves and an easygoing seafront.
destinations.html:
Protaras sits a short way north of Ayia Napa on the southeast coast, and runs a calmer, more family-oriented version of the same white-sand coastline. The resort spreads along a strip of hotels and apartments behind a chain of small, sheltered bays, with an easygoing seafront promenade rather than the dense club scene of its neighbour. It suits families and couples who want the clear water without the late-night crowds.

The centrepiece is Fig Tree Bay, a Blue Flag beach of fine white sand and shallow turquoise water, with a small rocky islet a short swim offshore. The coast either side is broken into a series of coves, many with sunbeds, watersports and easy snorkelling. The protected headland of Cape Greco lies just south, walkable along the coastal path, and the sheltered Konnos Bay sits between the two resorts.

What to do

  • Spend a beach day at Fig Tree Bay and snorkel out to the islet.
  • Walk the coastal path south toward Cape Greco and its sea caves.
  • Swim in the calm, clear water of Konnos Bay between the resorts.
  • Climb to the Profitis Ilias chapel above town for views over the coast.

The water along this stretch is shallow and gentle near shore, which makes it good for children and weaker swimmers. Evenings are low-key, centred on seafront restaurants and family entertainment rather than clubs. The shoulder months of May, June, September and October bring warm sea and fewer crowds.

Lively Ayia Napa is only about 10 to 12 kilometres south for those who want a night out, while Larnaca and its airport are roughly 45 minutes away. That mix of calm base and easy access makes Protaras a practical family choice.

destinations.name: Troodos Mountains
destinations.tagline: Central massif of painted churches, Mount Olympus and wine villages
destinations.summary: The Troodos Mountains are Cyprus's cool, forested interior: Mount Olympus, the UNESCO-listed painted churches, the hilltop Kykkos Monastery and stone wine villages.
destinations.html:
The Troodos Mountains form the forested central massif of Cyprus, a cool, pine-clad upland that contrasts sharply with the hot coast. Topped by Mount Olympus (Chionistra) at 1,952 metres, the highest point on the island, the range holds Byzantine churches, monasteries, stone villages and walking trails. In winter the upper slopes see enough snow for a small ski area; in summer they offer a cool retreat from the beaches.

The cultural highlight is a group of painted churches inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985 (now ten in total, the last added in 2001), whose interiors are covered with detailed Byzantine and post-Byzantine murals. The grand Kykkos Monastery, founded in the 11th century and richly decorated, sits high on the western slopes. Mount Olympus itself can be reached by road, with a nature trail looping near the summit.

What to do

  • Visit several of the UNESCO painted churches scattered through the hill villages.
  • Tour the hilltop Kykkos Monastery and its museum of icons and treasures.
  • Drive or walk near Mount Olympus, the island's highest summit.
  • Stroll the cobbled wine village of Omodos and stop at a family winery.

Resort and base villages such as Pano Platres and Troodos square sit high in the range, with tavernas, trails and waterfalls nearby. Lower down, wine villages on the southern slopes, including Omodos, produce local wines; Commandaria comes from a separate area of fourteen wine communities. The mountains reward a slow drive, with frequent stops for churches, viewpoints and food.

The Troodos make an easy day trip or overnight from the coast, climbing inland from Limassol and Paphos and reachable from the capital Nicosia. Bring a layer even in summer, as the air is noticeably cooler at altitude.

beaches.name: Blue Lagoon (Akamas)
beaches.tagline: Clear turquoise inlet reached by boat from Latchi
beaches.summary: A sheltered turquoise inlet on the northwest Akamas, usually reached by boat from Latchi. Clear, calm water for swimming and snorkelling. No paved road access.
beaches.html:
The Blue Lagoon is a sheltered inlet on the northwestern tip of the Akamas peninsula, in the Republic of Cyprus. (This is the Cyprus Akamas Blue Lagoon, not the separate site in the occupied north.) The water here is unusually clear and calm, shading from pale aqua near the rocks to deep turquoise offshore, which is why it has become the headline stop on boat trips along this coast.

There is no paved road to the lagoon. Most visitors arrive on a boat trip from Latchi harbour, a short drive west of Polis and around 45 minutes from Paphos, with day boats and smaller charters running through the season and stopping for a swim. The more adventurous reach it overland by 4x4 or on foot along the Akamas trails, though that is a rougher, longer way in. The lagoon itself has no facilities, so food, water and shade come with you (or with the boat), and it can get crowded with boats at the height of summer.

How to visit

  • Reached by boat from Latchi, or overland by 4x4 and on foot.
  • Clear, calm water that is good for swimming and snorkelling.
  • No sunbeds, kiosks or shade at the lagoon itself.
  • Boats stop for a timed swim; check how long your trip allows in the water.

A Blue Lagoon boat trip pairs well with the rest of an Akamas day: the springs at the Baths of Aphrodite and the start of the peninsula's coastal trails are near Latchi, while the turtle beach at Lara Beach and the gorge at Avakas Gorge lie on the Akamas coast toward Paphos.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: None at the lagoon; depart from Latchi harbour

beaches.name: Coral Bay
beaches.tagline: Crescent family beach north of Paphos
beaches.summary: A sheltered crescent of golden sand between two limestone headlands near Peyia, north of Paphos. Calm, shallow water and full facilities. Blue Flag beach.
beaches.html:
Coral Bay is the main resort beach of the Peyia area, a short drive north of Paphos. The beach is a crescent of soft golden sand, around 500 metres long, enclosed by a pair of low limestone headlands that shelter the bay and keep the water calm and shallow. That setting, plus the full range of facilities behind the sand, makes it the most popular family beach in the Paphos area. It holds Blue Flag status.

The shallow, gentle entry suits children and weaker swimmers, while the headlands at each end offer rockier spots for snorkelling. Sunbeds, umbrellas and watersports operate along the beach, and lifeguards are on duty during the main season. A strip of tavernas, cafes and shops sits just behind, so it is easy to spend a full day here without moving far. The bay can get busy at the height of summer, but the deep, soft sand and the protected water keep it a comfortable choice for a relaxed family day on the Paphos coast.

Visiting Coral Bay

  • Blue Flag beach with lifeguards through the summer season.
  • Sunbeds, umbrellas, showers, toilets and watersports on the sand.
  • Tavernas, cafes and shops line the road above the beach.
  • Rockier ends of the bay are good for snorkelling.

Coral Bay is a good base for the Paphos coast: the wild, undeveloped Lara Beach and the gorge walk at Avakas Gorge lie further north on the Akamas, while the city's Tombs of the Kings and Paphos Archaeological Park are a short drive south.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: Free and paid parking near the beach

beaches.name: Fig Tree Bay
beaches.tagline: Protaras's family bay with calm, shallow water
beaches.summary: Protaras's headline beach: a wide arc of pale sand, calm shallow water and a small offshore islet. A long-standing Blue Flag beach, good for families.
beaches.html:
Fig Tree Bay is the centre of Protaras and one of the most photographed beaches in Cyprus. A wide arc of soft, pale gold sand backs onto calm, shallow water, with a small rocky islet a short swim offshore that confident swimmers like to reach. The bay is named for an old fig tree near the shore.

The water shelves gently and stays clear and protected, which makes Fig Tree Bay a reliable family choice. Sunbeds and umbrellas fill much of the sand in summer, watersports operators run from the beach, and a strip of cafes, tavernas and hotels sits just behind. The bay is consistently ranked among the better beaches in Europe, which is part of why it draws steady crowds through the season. It gets busy at peak times, so arriving early gives you the calmest water and the best pick of space.

Planning a Fig Tree Bay day

  • Blue Flag beach with lifeguards through the main season.
  • Sunbeds, umbrellas, showers, toilets and watersports on the sand.
  • Tavernas, cafes and shops line the road behind the beach.
  • The offshore islet is a short swim for stronger swimmers only.

Fig Tree Bay sits along the Protaras strip near the sandy Sunrise Beach, with the sheltered Konnos Bay and the cliffs of Cape Greco a short drive south. The beaches of Ayia Napa, including Nissi Beach, are an easy hop along the coast.

photo.alt: Fig tree near Fig Tree Bay

beaches.name: Finikoudes Beach
beaches.summary: Larnaca's central beach along the palm-lined Finikoudes promenade, with calm shallow water and cafes, bars and the marina close by. A Blue Flag beach.
beaches.html:
Finikoudes is the central seafront beach of Larnaca, running along the palm-lined promenade that gives it its name (foinikoudes means little palm trees in Greek). The sand is fine and varies from brown to beige, and the water is calm and shallow, sheltered between the marina and fishing harbour at one end and a pier near the medieval fort at the other. It holds Blue Flag status and is the easiest beach to reach on foot in the city.

The big draw is the setting. The promenade behind the sand is lined with cafes, tavernas, bars and palm trees, so you can step straight off the beach into the heart of Larnaca's seafront life. Sunbeds, umbrellas, showers and changing rooms are on the sand, and lifeguards are on duty in the main season. The marina and fishing harbour at one end and the medieval fort at the other bookend the beach and are worth a wander. It is family friendly and central, which also means it is one of the busier beaches in the city through the summer.

Visiting Finikoudes

  • Blue Flag beach in the centre of Larnaca, easy to reach on foot.
  • Sunbeds, umbrellas, showers and changing rooms on the sand.
  • Cafes, tavernas and bars line the palm-lined promenade behind.
  • A coastal walkway links Finikoudes with Mackenzie Beach to the south.

Finikoudes is close to the Church of Saint Lazarus in the old town, while the Larnaca Salt Lake lies southwest of the city. For a livelier, bar-heavy stretch of sand, follow the seafront south to Mackenzie Beach.

facts.label: Parking
facts.value: Paid city parking near the promenade
